arXiv:2610.18082v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026

Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling
for Long-Horizon Agents

Xiyang Wu* Affiliation: University of Maryland    Zhichao Liu* Affiliation: University of Maryland    Shengxin Zhang* Affiliation: Google    Zongxia Li Affiliation: University of Maryland    Ming Li Affiliation: University of Maryland    Tianyi Zhou Affiliation: MBZUAI    Dinesh Manocha Affiliation: University of Maryland
Abstract

Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BeliefWeaver, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BeliefWeaver improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Long-horizon agents tackle tasks such as autonomous research Yamada et al. (2025), computer use Xie et al. (2024), and sequential decision-making Yao et al. (2022). However, early mistakes can propagate through long trajectories, trapping agents in repetitive attempts or leading to premature commitments that are difficult to reverse Wang et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2026b); Li et al. (2026). The evidence needed to identify these mistakes often emerges only after many subsequent actions. Recovering from such failures requires agents to revisit earlier assumptions in light of new evidence and use what they learn to guide subsequent exploration.

Reflection allows agents to revise their behavior after failures or new evidence Shinn et al. (2023); Madaan et al. (2023). Recovery may involve backtracking and trying another frontier, a testable hypothesis for repairing the current failure. Existing approaches often organize such alternatives as a tree to support branching and backtracking Zhu et al. (2026); Chen et al. (2026); Jin et al. (2026). Long-horizon failures, however, can arise from earlier decisions or assumptions shared across branches Zhuang et al. (2026); Rafi et al. (2026). Although rollback and persistent memory can preserve what happened, recovery still requires deciding how new verifier-grounded evidence should change the priorities of related repair hypotheses. When frontiers share prerequisites or interact across steps, evidence from one attempt can make another direction more or less promising Zhang et al. (2026d); Liang et al. (2026). This motivates a persistent exploration state that carries evidence across rollback and uses it to reprioritize future exploration.

We represent exploration as a persistent relational state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Recorded outcomes and candidate relations determine which unary evidence factors update each frontier’s priority Mishra et al. (2024); Cao and Chen (2026). This lets evidence from one attempt re-rank related alternatives, while diagnostic evidence separately controls execution eligibility. The state is preserved across rollback. Belief updates capture what has been learned, but recovery also requires deciding what to try next. Recent agentic world models Zuo et al. (2026) use learned dynamics or outcome prediction to guide decisions Zhou et al. (2024); Zhao et al. (2026). We use an implicit world model (IWM) to evaluate repair hypotheses, estimate prospective progress, and infer frontier relations, guiding their generation, refinement, and reconsideration. These repeated assessments can then be distilled into a lightweight student to reduce teacher inference cost Yang et al. (2026).

In this paper, we introduce BeliefWeaver, a framework for long-horizon problem solving that combines a persistent relational exploration state with an implicit world model (IWM). The exploration state tracks frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints, preserving evidence across rollback and using new outcomes to revise related hypotheses. The IWM evaluates repair hypotheses, estimates prospective progress, and infers relations among frontiers to guide what to explore next. Execution outcomes are then added back to the persistent state, so later decisions can build on earlier attempts. Because these assessments are used repeatedly during exploration, we distill them into a lightweight 9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and on-policy distillation (OPD) Agarwal et al. (2024), improving task performance while reducing teacher API costs Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025). This makes recovery cumulative: failed attempts provide evidence for subsequent exploration rather than simply triggering another retry. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce a recovery controller that uses retained execution evidence and relations among repair hypotheses to update frontier priorities. It can reprioritize candidates beyond the latest attempt, while a separate diagnostic gate controls execution eligibility.

  • •

    We develop an implicit world model that reasons over repair hypotheses, expected progress, and their relations, and distill this reasoning into a smaller student for efficient execution.

  • •

    Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BeliefWeaver improves aggregate final score by 5.1 points over native Terminus-2 continuation and also improves exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student gains 9.8 points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8%.

2 Related Work

World Models for Agentic Reasoning. World models let agents reason about possible future outcomes before acting. Prior work has explored both implicit predictive models and explicit executable ones. FLARE Zheng et al. (2025) predicts latent future observations for robot control, while Qwen-AgentWorld Zuo et al. (2026) models agent–environment transitions for general-purpose agents. RAP Hao et al. (2023) and WebDreamer Gu et al. (2024) use LLMs to predict outcomes during planning, and WKM Qiao et al. (2024) combines global task knowledge with local state. Other work builds executable models for internal simulation, including WorldCoder Tang et al. (2024) and Executable World Models Rodionov (2026); PatchWorld Bai et al. (2026), OPINE-World Courtis et al. (2026), and Tycho Lehmann et al. (2026) further support inspection, replay, and revision. Our work instead uses consequence predictions and verifier feedback to maintain a persistent belief over unresolved frontiers and guide exploration across them.

Long-horizon and Recursive Agents. Long-horizon agents face context growth, evidence loss, error propagation, and difficulty recovering from earlier decisions Chen et al. (2026); Zhu et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2026a). Recent work addresses these issues through persistent state, structured search, recursion, and recovery. Argus Zhang et al. (2026e) uses a shared evidence graph to coordinate search. HTR Jin et al. (2026) maintains a persistent tree of hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and insights, propagating experimental findings to refine and guide later search. AgentRewind Zhuang et al. (2026) restores earlier checkpoints while retaining memories from failed attempts. Recursive Language Models Zhang et al. (2025) recurse over subproblems, while Recursive Agent Harnesses Lumer et al. (2026) extend this to tool-using subagents. SciNav Zhang and Sun (2026) frames scientific coding as search over alternative solution branches. Our controller turns retained outcomes and frontier relations into explicit priority updates through unary evidence factors, including for candidates not executed in the latest attempt. A separate diagnostic gate determines which frontiers are eligible for execution.

Self-Improving and Uncertainty-Guided Agents. Recent agents increasingly learn from accumulated experience or use uncertainty to decide what to explore next. SkillRL Xia et al. (2026) jointly evolves a hierarchical skill library and agent policy, while COS-PLAY Wu et al. (2026) discovers and refines reusable skills from interaction trajectories. Darwin Gödel Machine Zhang et al. (2026a), Gödel Agent Yin et al. (2025), and Hyperagents Zhang et al. (2026b) go further by iteratively modifying the agent’s code, logic, or improvement process. MLEvolve Du et al. (2026) combines cross-branch search with retrospective memory, while Uncertainty-Guided Tree Search Mhammedi and Cohan (2026) and Agentic Uncertainty Zhang et al. (2026c) use epistemic uncertainty to guide exploration and reflection. Our work instead uses verifier-grounded evidence to update priorities over related frontiers, allowing the agent to revisit promising directions without changing the underlying agent.

3 Problem Formulation

Long-Horizon Problem Solving as Frontier Exploration. We consider an agent operating in a partially observable long-horizon environment, where decisions are conditioned on the interaction history hth_{t}. Instead of modeling individual low-level actions, we formulate exploration over a time-varying set of problem-solving frontiers,

ℱt={f1,…,fNt}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{t}=\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{N_{t}}\}.

Each frontier fif_{i} is a testable repair hypothesis that specifies a possible failure mechanism, the evidence needed to assess it, and the checks used to evaluate the repair. At step tt, the agent either explores an eligible frontier or continues execution to gather evidence that can support, refine, or introduce new frontiers. The set ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} evolves over time, while ii identifies the same frontier across repeated attempts.

Persistent Exploration State. We maintain a relational graph

Gt=(Vt,ℛt),\displaystyle G_{t}=(V_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t}),

where VtV_{t} is the node set and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} is the relation edge set. The graph connects frontiers with their attempts, observations, and checkpoints, and links frontiers that share or refine failure mechanisms. For each frontier fif_{i}, we maintain a belief

bti=qti​(zi=1),\displaystyle b_{t}^{i}=q_{t}^{i}(z_{i}=1),

where zi∈{0,1}z_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the frontier remains worth pursuing and qtiq_{t}^{i} is the corresponding belief distribution. We summarize the exploration state as

Bt=(Gt,ℰt,𝐛t),𝐛t=(bti)fi∈ℱt,\displaystyle B_{t}=(G_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},\mathbf{b}_{t}),\qquad\mathbf{b}_{t}=(b_{t}^{i})_{f_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}},

where ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} contains accumulated diagnostic observations and execution feedback. Relations in GtG_{t} determine which observations activate unary evidence factors for each frontier, allowing new evidence to update the priority of related hypotheses beyond the latest attempt. New evidence et+1e_{t+1} is incorporated through

Bt+1=Update⁡(Bt,et+1).\displaystyle B_{t+1}=\operatorname{Update}(B_{t},e_{t+1}).

The exploration state persists across environment rollback, so evidence from earlier attempts remains available for subsequent decisions.

Implicit World Modeling of Exploration. Belief updates summarize what has already been learned from exploration, while choosing how to proceed requires reasoning about unexplored directions. We model this prospective reasoning with an implicit world model (IWM),

ψθ​(Bt,fi)=(d^ti,p^ti,r^ti),\displaystyle\psi_{\theta}(B_{t},f_{i})=\big(\hat{d}_{t}^{i},\hat{p}_{t}^{i},\hat{r}_{t}^{i}\big),

which assesses a candidate frontier fif_{i} under the current exploration state BtB_{t}. Here, d^ti\hat{d}_{t}^{i} evaluates the hypothesis against available evidence, p^ti\hat{p}_{t}^{i} estimates its potential for repair progress, and r^ti\hat{r}_{t}^{i} captures its relations to other frontiers. These assessments guide frontier eligibility and belief revision, connect evidence across related hypotheses, and support frontier generation, refinement, and reopening. The model is implicit because it reasons directly from the exploration context rather than learning an explicit transition model of the environment.

Exploration Objective. The goal of exploration is to make sustained progress toward task completion under a limited execution budget. At each step, the agent uses the accumulated evidence and frontier beliefs in BtB_{t} to maintain and prioritize plausible frontiers, while allowing earlier hypotheses to be revisited as new evidence emerges. When no frontier is ready to pursue, execution continues to gather evidence and expose new repair directions. The resulting feedback supplies new evidence et+1e_{t+1} for updating the exploration state. The concrete gating and ranking rules are introduced in the next section.

4 Methodology

We propose BeliefWeaver, a framework for long-horizon problem solving that organizes exploration around testable repair hypotheses and evidence-grounded beliefs over which directions remain worth pursuing (Figure 1). An Implicit World Model proposes and evaluates candidate frontiers using targeted diagnostics and estimates of repair progress, while a Persistent Global Belief State tracks their evidence and relations across attempts and rollback. Diagnostic evidence determines which frontiers are eligible for execution, and belief scores rank the remaining candidates. Execution outcomes are then added back to the state, allowing failed attempts to reshape related hypotheses and reconsider previously deprioritized alternatives. To reduce repeated teacher inference, we distill four recurring IWM roles into a 9B student while keeping the recovery controller and executor unchanged.

4.1 Implicit World Model

The implicit world model (IWM) represents unresolved failures as structured hypotheses over possible mechanisms and repairs. For each hypothesis, it asks three questions: what may be causing the failure, whether the available evidence supports that explanation, and what progress is expected from pursuing the repair.

Candidate Hypothesis Generation. For each unresolved failure, a language model receives the task requirements, line-indexed source context, current diagnostics, and previous attempts, and proposes a testable repair hypothesis. Each proposal describes a mismatch between the implementation and specification, a possible underlying mechanism, relevant source locations, evidence to collect, and a target check. Valid proposals are added to the frontier catalog for later evaluation.

Diagnostic Probing and Evidence Judgment. For each candidate, the controller generates a diagnostic command and runs it in a temporary copy of the current environment. An evidence judge compares the observation with the candidate’s predicted current behavior and returns

vti∈{consistent,insufficient,contradicted}.v_{t}^{i}\in\{\texttt{consistent},\texttt{insufficient},\texttt{contradicted}\}.

The verdict determines execution eligibility, while contradictions also add refutation evidence to the belief state.

Prospective Evaluation. Two prompt-based experts estimate the consequences of pursuing each hypothesis. local_code traces the relevant control and data flow to estimate mechanism validity and progress under a bounded repair attempt, while contract_judge checks whether the current implementation violates the cited task requirement. Their outputs are combined into an estimate of strict progress using the mechanism selection and outcome composition in Appendix D.3. Relation queries also identify refinements and shared mechanisms among candidates, connecting unsuccessful attempts to related hypotheses.

Evidence verdicts determine execution eligibility and update beliefs, while candidate relations determine which relational evidence factors apply. Prospective estimates are used for candidate regeneration and conditional reopening. Selectable frontiers are ultimately ordered by the belief score in Section 4.2. Prompt templates, thresholds, and update rules are given in Appendix A.1.

4.2 Persistent Global Belief State

Long-horizon recovery often returns to earlier checkpoints after unsuccessful interventions. We maintain a persistent belief state over repair hypotheses and their evidence so that outcomes from previous attempts can shape what to explore next.

We represent this state as an exploration graph GtG_{t} over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Each attempt is linked to the frontier it pursues and its starting checkpoint, while frontier–frontier relations capture shared mechanisms and hypothesis refinements. The graph and its evidence persist across rollback.

For each frontier fif_{i}, we introduce a binary variable ziz_{i} indicating whether it remains active for exploration. Starting from a neutral prior, we aggregate the evidence associated with fif_{i} as

qti​(zi)=1Zti​ϕ0i​(zi)​∏a∈𝒜tiψa​(zi,ℰt,Gt),q_{t}^{i}(z_{i})=\frac{1}{Z_{t}^{i}}\phi_{0}^{i}(z_{i})\prod_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{i}}\psi_{a}(z_{i};\mathcal{E}_{t},G_{t}), (1)

where ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} is the accumulated evidence, 𝒜ti\mathcal{A}_{t}^{i} indexes the factors applicable to frontier ii, and ZtiZ_{t}^{i} is the normalization constant. We use bti=qti​(zi=1)b_{t}^{i}=q_{t}^{i}(z_{i}=1) as the frontier priority for subsequent exploration.

Relations in GtG_{t} determine which unary evidence factors apply to each frontier. This lets an outcome from one attempt change the priority of a related frontier, while each belief is computed independently by local normalization.

We use four types of evidence: repeated attempts, refinements, historical target feedback, and probe-based refutation. Repeated failures lower the priority of the same frontier, while an untried refinement can remain promising. Historical target feedback downweights candidates whose targets have not improved in earlier attempts, and contradictory probe observations provide direct refutation evidence. Full factor definitions and parameter settings are given in Appendix A.2.

4.3 Evidence-Gated Execution

The controller uses the persistent belief state to decide which frontier should guide the next execution. Open or reopened frontiers are ranked by

St​(fi)=bti−λfail​ℓti,S_{t}(f_{i})=b_{t}^{i}-\lambda_{\mathrm{fail}}\,\ell_{t}^{i}, (2)

where ℓti\ell_{t}^{i} indicates that the frontier’s most recent queue outcome is failure.

Ranking and execution eligibility are handled separately. Before execution, a frontier must receive a consistent evidence verdict and have a target that is not already satisfied. The highest-ranked eligible frontier is passed to the agent harness with its supporting evidence and execution context. If none qualifies, the agent continues without a frontier-specific focus.

The verifier then scores the resulting state. Improving checkpoints are retained, while unsuccessful updates are rolled back. In either case, the new observations and attempt history are added to the persistent state. Algorithm 1 summarizes the recovery loop from frontier selection through execution, verification, and state update. Additional fallback and checkpoint-retention rules are given in Appendix A.3.

4.4 Small-Model IWM Distillation

The IWM relies on four recurring model-assisted roles: probe generation, evidence judgment, frontier-relation inference, and task-clause assessment. These roles use structured inputs and outputs and account for much of the repeated teacher inference, so we distill them into a smaller student model.

We first train the student with SFT using LoRA Hu et al. (2022) on teacher-generated, role-specific request–response pairs. This gives the student the basic behavior and output structure needed to participate in exploration.

SFT covers states collected under teacher-guided exploration. We therefore use on-policy distillation (OPD) to train on contexts induced by the student’s own decisions. During collection, the student handles the four distilled roles, while a shadow teacher answers the same requests for supervision without replacing the student’s outputs. These teacher-labeled examples are combined with the SFT data and earlier OPD rounds, and training continues from the latest accepted adapter. After validation, the updated student is used for the next collection round.

Only these recurring IWM roles are transferred to the student; the recovery controller, executor, belief-update rules, and prospective evaluation remain unchanged. Training details and validation criteria are provided in Appendix B.

5 Results

5.1 Experimental Setup

Experiment Design. We conduct two sets of experiments. First, using DeepSeek V4 Pro Xu et al. (2026), we evaluate the contributions of structured continuation, world-model grounding, and persistent relational beliefs through controlled ablations. Second, we distill these capabilities into Qwen3.5-9B Qwen Team (2026), comparing different distillation strategies in terms of task performance and teacher inference cost.

Benchmarks. We evaluate on 113 tasks from three terminal-based benchmarks: 65 from Terminal-Bench 2.0 (TB2), 23 from Terminal-Bench 3.0 (TB3) Merrill et al. (2026), and 25 from Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench (LHTB) Li et al. (2026). TB2 and TB3 cover diverse terminal tasks with test-based feedback, while LHTB emphasizes longer-horizon execution and provides score-only feedback. Together, they test recovery across different task lengths and levels of diagnostic information. Full task and evaluation details are given in Appendix C.

Baselines. We compare four configurations that progressively add components of BeliefWeaver: (1) Terminus-2, the native continuation baseline; (2) + Structured Continuation, adding checkpointing, candidate execution, and rollback; (3) + WM Grounding, adding diagnostic probes, execution feedback, and candidate-specific target checks; and (4) full BeliefWeaver, adding persistent relational beliefs and evidence-gated execution. All configurations start from the same checkpoint with the same remaining execution budget.

Distillation. We evaluate three variants using Qwen3.5-9B Qwen Team (2026). SFT is trained on teacher responses, SFT + OPD adds teacher supervision collected during student-guided exploration, and SFT + OPD + Gen also lets the student generate repair hypotheses.

The student handles probe generation, evidence judgment, candidate-relation inference, and task-clause assessment in all three settings. Repair hypotheses remain teacher-generated for SFT and SFT + OPD, while SFT + OPD + Gen generates them with the student. Prospective evaluation remains teacher-based.

Both SFT and OPD train LoRA adapters with response-token cross-entropy while keeping the base model frozen. Each OPD round adds new teacher-labeled examples to the SFT data and earlier OPD data. All variants use the same executor and belief-update rules. API savings are measured against the matched teacher run. Training data and hyperparameters are given in Appendix B.

Evaluation protocol and metrics. For each paired comparison, methods start from the same checkpoint and receive the same remaining execution budget. We report Final as the test-pass fraction or graded reward of the final retained checkpoint (%). Step-AUC and Time-AUC summarize performance over agent steps and executor time, using a shared per-task step horizon and the remaining execution-time budget, respectively. Both are normalized and scaled by 100. We also track executor usage, execution time, and controller or teacher API usage during continuation. All metrics are averaged equally across tasks, with Overall pooling tasks across benchmarks. Additional accounting and evaluation details are provided in Appendix C.

5.2 Main Results

Improved task performance and exploration efficiency. Compared with native Terminus-2 continuation, BeliefWeaver improves Overall Final performance by 5.1 percentage points, with the largest gain on TB3 (+10.1 points). It also improves Overall Step-AUC by 2.8 points and Time-AUC by 1.6 points, achieving the strongest aggregate results among the teacher configurations. The gains in Final and Step-AUC are significant relative to the native baseline (Table 2). Together, these results show that BeliefWeaver not only reaches better retained checkpoints, but also makes useful progress earlier during continuation. This pattern is consistent with more effective recovery rather than gains appearing only at the end of execution.

Component ablations support the combined design. We use component ablations to examine the role of each stage in the full framework. Structured Continuation improves Overall Final, Step-AUC, and Time-AUC over Terminus-2 by 2.9, 0.9, and 1.1 points, respectively. Adding WM Grounding alone reduces Overall Final by 1.7 points, with small declines in both AUC metrics. Adding persistent relational beliefs and evidence-gated execution on top of grounding improves Overall Final by 3.9 points, along with gains of 2.4 in Step-AUC and 1.0 in Time-AUC. The best results come from using grounding together with the full recovery controller, which updates frontier priorities from retained evidence and separately gates execution with diagnostic evidence. Since these two components are introduced together, their individual effects are not isolated.

Executor savings come with greater controller overhead. Table 3 compares resource usage across the four teacher configurations. We report executor steps, execution time, logged executor cost, and controller reservations per task. Compared with Terminus-2, BeliefWeaver reduces executor steps by 13.2%, execution time by 17.8%, and executor cost by 16.6%, while achieving a higher Final score. The full system uses slightly more executor resources than the intermediate ablations but attains the best task performance. It also requires more controller calls, with 33.4 reservations per task compared with 9.1 or fewer for the other configurations. This motivates distilling the recurring IWM roles to reduce teacher usage. The savings in this table refer to executor resources; teacher API savings are reported separately below.

5.3 Distillation Results

Distillation transfers the recurring IWM decisions, while OPD yields a higher final score. We next ask whether the model-assisted IWM roles can be moved to a smaller student without losing the benefits of evidence-guided recovery. SFT already improves substantially over native Terminus-2, suggesting that these structured decisions can be learned from teacher supervision rather than requiring the full teacher at every step. OPD then trains the student on contexts produced by its own exploration. SFT + OPD reaches 58.4% Overall Final, 9.8 points above the native baseline, with a significant Final gain (Table 2). Its Final point estimate is also 4.7 points above the matched teacher. This suggests that on-policy supervision can do more than reproduce teacher outputs: it can adapt the distilled IWM roles to the states the student actually encounters during recovery. Overall, the results support a simple division of labor: SFT provides the structured IWM behavior, while OPD adapts it to the student’s exploration distribution. The recovery controller and executor remain unchanged, so the gains come from replacing and refining the recurring model-assisted decisions rather than distilling the entire agent.

Student-generated hypotheses yield the largest teacher savings. We assess distillation efficiency using executor time, teacher API requests, and estimated API cost from recorded token usage at $1/$4 per million input/output tokens. Across the tasks in Table 4, both SFT and SFT + OPD cut teacher requests and API cost by about 55% relative to the matched teacher. Moving repair-hypothesis generation to the student yields larger savings: SFT + OPD + Gen reduces teacher requests by 74.5% and API cost by 81.9%, lowering the average teacher cost from $0.550 to $0.100 per task. It also reaches 57.5% Final, 3.8 points above the matched teacher. Teacher token usage follows the same pattern, decreasing by 55.4%, 55.1%, and 81.1% for SFT, SFT + OPD, and SFT + OPD + Gen, respectively. Overall, distillation substantially reduces teacher inference while maintaining strong task performance, with the largest savings when hypothesis generation is also moved to the student. These savings refer to teacher API usage rather than total end-to-end inference cost.

6 Conclusion

We presented BeliefWeaver, a framework for long-horizon failure recovery built around an evidence-guided recovery controller. The controller carries verifier-grounded evidence across attempts and rollback, uses relations among repair hypotheses to update frontier priorities, and separates execution eligibility from belief-based ranking. An implicit world model supports this process by generating and evaluating repair hypotheses, estimating prospective progress, and identifying relations among frontiers. Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BeliefWeaver improves task performance and exploration efficiency over native continuation. Distilling the recurring controller roles into a smaller student substantially reduces teacher API usage and cost while preserving strong task performance. Future work will study learned and uncertainty-aware belief updates, finer attribution among controller components, and recovery under sparse feedback or imperfect rollback.

Limitations

Our framework has several limitations. Errors in IWM predictions or inferred relations can mis-rank frontiers and waste exploration effort. The current belief state also models only a small set of relations between repair hypotheses, which may be too limited when several failure causes interact. Finally, our experiments focus on terminal-based tasks with verifier feedback and reliable checkpoint restoration. It remains unclear how well the framework transfers to settings where feedback is sparse or rollback is noisy or unavailable.

Appendix A Controller Details

Table 5 summarizes the controller settings used throughout the experiments. The following subsections describe how these settings enter belief updates, frontier selection, and execution.

A.1 Implicit World Model

Candidate generation. The generator receives the task requirements, line-indexed source context, current diagnostics, existing candidates, and previous attempts. It returns structured repair hypotheses containing a proposed mechanism, the observed and required behavior, supporting source references, evidence to collect, a target check, and an optional parent candidate. The controller validates the required fields and references before adding them to the frontier catalog.

Probes and evidence verdicts. For each candidate, a separate model call generates a diagnostic command from the hypothesis and requested evidence. The command is executed in a temporary checkpoint copy, subject to the timeout and output-retention limits in Table 5. The evidence judge compares the observed output and return code against the candidate’s claimed current behavior: consistent indicates supporting evidence, contradicted indicates conflicting evidence, and insufficient is used when the probe does not resolve the claim. These verdicts are used by the evidence factors and execution gate described in Appendices A.2 and A.3.

Prospective evaluation and relations. The local_code expert estimates mechanism validity and expected repair progress from the relevant control and data flow, while contract_judge checks the current implementation against the cited task requirement. A separate relation query identifies links such as same_mechanism and supports between candidates. These signals guide candidate regeneration and frontier reopening as exploration progresses, using the thresholds in Table 5.

A.2 Evidence Factors and Belief Updates

Factor model.

Each frontier has a binary active/inactive variable with uniform prior. Applicable evidence is represented by unary odds factors, giving

Oti\displaystyle O_{t}^{i} =λattnti​λrelrti​λtgtuti​λctrcti,\displaystyle=\lambda_{\mathrm{att}}^{\,n_{t}^{i}}\lambda_{\mathrm{rel}}^{\,r_{t}^{i}}\lambda_{\mathrm{tgt}}^{\,u_{t}^{i}}\lambda_{\mathrm{ctr}}^{\,c_{t}^{i}}, (3)
bti\displaystyle b_{t}^{i} =Oti1+Oti,\displaystyle=\frac{O_{t}^{i}}{1+O_{t}^{i}}, (4)

where factor values are listed in Table 5. Candidate relations determine which unary factors apply to each frontier, but do not introduce pairwise potentials between frontier variables. Given the recorded graph and evidence, we therefore compute each frontier belief independently by local normalization. These beliefs are used to rank exploration frontiers rather than as calibrated estimates of mechanism correctness or repair success.

Let 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} denote frontiers whose latest outcome is a failure or that have a recorded non-improving focused attempt. With queue attempt count NtiN_{t}^{i},

nti={max⁡(1,Nti),fi∈𝒟t,0,otherwise.n_{t}^{i}=\begin{cases}\max(1,N_{t}^{i}),&f_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{t},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

For an unfailed frontier, rti=1r_{t}^{i}=1 when its parent is in 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} or it is linked to a member of 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} by same_mechanism or supports; otherwise rti=0r_{t}^{i}=0. The relation factor is applied once per frontier. Similarly, uti=1u_{t}^{i}=1 when an unfailed frontier targets a component previously modified by a focused attempt, and cti=1c_{t}^{i}=1 when its retained evidence verdict is contradicted. Target-history markers persist across rollback, while contradiction state is updated when new evidence becomes available.

Parameter choice.

We set λatt=0.34\lambda_{\mathrm{att}}=0.34 from development retry statistics: unsuccessful candidates improved substantially less often when revisited than other executed candidates. The remaining factor values are fixed on development data and listed in Table 5.

A.3 Evidence-Gated Execution

Selection and gating.

Only open or reopened frontiers are considered for execution. Candidates are ranked by

St​(fi)=bti−λfail​ℓti,S_{t}(f_{i})=b_{t}^{i}-\lambda_{\mathrm{fail}}\ell_{t}^{i}, (5)

where ℓti\ell_{t}^{i} indicates whether the most recent attempt on fif_{i} failed and λfail\lambda_{\mathrm{fail}} is given in Table 5. The controller selects the highest-ranked candidate with a current consistent evidence verdict whose target is not already passing. Blocking verifier failures take precedence and trigger continuation aimed at restoring execution or producing the required deliverable. If no frontier passes the evidence gate, or exploration stagnates, the controller falls back to plain continuation.

Execution.

For a selected frontier, the agent receives the task, current verification state, repair hypothesis, supporting evidence, and relevant attempt history. Plain continuation uses the same executor without frontier-specific context. After verification, improved checkpoints are retained and otherwise the environment is rolled back, while accumulated evidence and exploration history persist for subsequent belief updates.

Appendix B Distillation Data and Training

Distillation setup. We distill four roles into a shared Qwen3.5-9B student: probe generation, evidence judgment, candidate-relation inference, and task-clause assessment. SFT and SFT + OPD retain teacher-based hypothesis generation, while SFT + OPD + Gen adds a separate generation adapter trained from the SFT checkpoint alongside the OPD adapter. Prospective evaluation remains teacher-based, with belief updates, execution gating, and task execution unchanged. Final evaluation tasks are excluded from SFT and OPD data collection, hypothesis-generation training, and development-based model selection. Training configurations are summarized in Table 6.

B.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

Data. We collect 859 SFT examples from 91 tasks across TB2, TB3 Merrill et al. (2026), and LHTB Li et al. (2026), using DeepSeek V4 Pro Xu et al. (2026) as the teacher. Each example preserves the original request context, tool schema, and structured teacher response. We use a task-level split of 723 training and 136 development examples.

SFT Warm Start. We train on the teacher’s structured responses with response-token cross-entropy, using the same chat template and tool-call format as at inference time. Sampling is balanced across task–role groups, with OPD additionally upweighting teacher–student disagreements. We train LoRA adapters with the base model frozen and discard examples beyond the context limit in Table 6. Each run uses one nominal epoch, with 5% linear warmup followed by linear decay to 0.1×0.1\times the initial learning rate. We retain the checkpoint with the lowest development loss.

B.2 On-Policy Distillation

Collection and weighting. OPD starts from the SFT student and follows the round and task allocation in Table 6. For each task, teacher-reference and student-assisted runs start from the same initial checkpoint. The student serves the four distilled roles, while a shadow teacher labels the same requests; failed student calls may fall back to the teacher. We retain valid teacher-labeled examples from student-induced contexts, teacher-reference runs, and fallback calls, and deduplicate identical request–target pairs within each batch. Examples are upweighted when student and teacher disagree on evidence verdicts or on same_mechanism/supports relations, in addition to the task–role balancing used for SFT.

Iterative updates and evaluation. At round kk, we train on the original SFT data together with the retained OPD data from rounds 1,…,k1,\ldots,k, starting from the latest accepted adapter. Training uses the same response-token objective as SFT, with checkpoint selection on the combined development set. After each round, we evaluate the adapter on the fixed SFT development set. We retain it if parser acceptance is at least 95% for every distilled role and its evidence-verdict agreement with the teacher is within 2 percentage points of the previous accepted adapter, where AprevA_{\mathrm{prev}} denotes the latter agreement (Table 6). The retained adapter is then used for the next round of data collection. The final student is the adapter retained after the last round, and we evaluate it from fresh initial checkpoints on the full downstream benchmarks using the same controller and execution protocol.

Hypothesis-generation extension. SFT + OPD + Gen combines the final OPD adapter for the four controller roles with a separate hypothesis-generation adapter initialized from SFT. The generator replaces teacher-based candidate generation, proposing testable failure mechanisms and repair directions based on task requirements, code context, and execution feedback. It is trained on teacher request–hypothesis pairs using response-token cross-entropy. After filtering sequences longer than 65,536 tokens, the dataset contains 609 training and 150 validation examples. Training runs for one epoch at a learning rate of 10−510^{-5} (Table 6).

Downstream evaluation. We evaluate the matched teacher and student configurations from the same initial checkpoints under identical execution budgets and verification procedures. All configurations share the same executor, controller logic, and belief-update rules, differing only in model-role assignments. Shadow-teacher labeling and teacher fallback are disabled during evaluation. Task coverage and metrics are detailed in Appendix C.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol and Metrics

C.1 Evaluation Procedure

Tasks and shared settings. We evaluate 113 tasks: 65 from TB2, 23 from TB3, and 25 from LHTB. For each task, we run the executor until its first stop or half the total execution-time budget, then initialize all continuation methods from the same checkpoint. All methods share the executor, environment, verification procedure, and remaining budget. TB2 and TB3 provide scores and failing-test names, while LHTB provides scores only. For student evaluation, we rerun the matched teacher alongside SFT, SFT + OPD, and SFT + OPD + Gen from shared checkpoints, with shadow-teacher labeling and teacher fallback disabled. To ensure task separation, we exclude all evaluation tasks from SFT and OPD data collection, hypothesis-generation training, and development-based model selection.

Execution budgets. Each task ii has a total executor-time budget:

Bi={min⁡(Biofficial,1800)​s,TB2,1200​s,TB3,720​s,LHTB.B_{i}=\begin{cases}\min(B_{i}^{\mathrm{official}},1800)\ \mathrm{s},&\text{TB2},\\ 1200\ \mathrm{s},&\text{TB3},\\ 720\ \mathrm{s},&\text{LHTB}.\end{cases}

For TB2, budgets range from 600 to 1,800 seconds, depending on the task. The same budgets apply to teacher and student evaluations. After the initial execution consumes ti,0t_{i,0} seconds, each method receives the remaining Bi−ti,0B_{i}-t_{i,0} seconds. Only executor time counts toward the budget. A continuation already running when the budget is exhausted may finish, while any continuation started afterward is excluded from scoring.

C.2 Metric Computation

Final score. Final measures task performance at the last retained checkpoint, excluding rejected trials. For checkpoints with multiple tests, we compute the score as max⁡(r,p/(p+f))\max(r,p/(p+f)), where rr is the official reward and pp and ff are the numbers of passed and failed tests. For single-score tasks, including LHTB, or checkpoints without test counts, we use the official graded reward. Final scores are reported as percentages.

Step-AUC. Step-AUC measures task progress over executor agent steps. Let ni,kn_{i,k} denote the number of agent steps in continuation round kk and qi,kq_{i,k} the retained score after that round, with qi,0q_{i,0} denoting the initial score. For this metric, we use the test-pass fraction for multi-test checkpoints and the official reward otherwise. Agent steps are counted from trajectory entries attributed to the executor agent. For KiK_{i} continuation rounds and Ni=∑k=1Kini,kN_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}n_{i,k} steps,

AUCistep\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}^{\mathrm{step}}_{i} =∑k=1Kini,k​qi,k−1+(Hi−Ni)​qi,KiHi.\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}n_{i,k}q_{i,k-1}+(H_{i}-N_{i})q_{i,K_{i}}}{H_{i}}. (6)

where HiH_{i} is the maximum continuation step count across the evaluated settings for task ii. The retained score remains constant during each round and is carried forward to the common horizon HiH_{i}.

Time-AUC. Time-AUC measures task progress over executor time. Let qi​(t)q_{i}(t) denote the latest retained checkpoint score at time tt, computed using the Final-score definition and held constant between checkpoints. We compute

AUCitime\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}^{\mathrm{time}}_{i} =∫ti,0Biqi​(t)​𝑑tmax⁡(1,Bi−ti,0),\displaystyle=\frac{\int_{t_{i,0}}^{B_{i}}q_{i}(t)\,dt}{\max(1,B_{i}-t_{i,0})}, (7)

where ti,0t_{i,0} marks the start of continuation and BiB_{i} is the total executor-time budget. The integral is computed over the piecewise-constant score curve, with the last retained score carried forward to BiB_{i} if execution ends early. Time is measured using executor runtime, excluding controller inference and orchestration overhead. Both AUC metrics are reported as percentages, with higher values indicating earlier progress.

Executor resources. We aggregate executor steps, runtime, and cost across all continuation attempts, including rejected trials. Shared executions are counted for each setting that uses them. Runtime is measured in seconds and excludes the initial execution, controller inference, verification, and orchestration. If a round exceeds the execution budget, its full runtime and cost are included. Executor cost is calculated from the USD charges recorded in agent trajectories.

Controller and teacher API usage. Controller usage is measured by non-executor API reservations, including unresolved requests. Teacher API requests are counted from reservations for teacher-served roles, with token usage matched by reservation ID. Let IiI_{i} and OiO_{i} denote the total input and output tokens from matched successful teacher calls for task ii. We estimate teacher API cost as

Citeacher\displaystyle C_{i}^{\mathrm{teacher}} =Ii+4​Oi106,\displaystyle=\frac{I_{i}+4O_{i}}{10^{6}}, (8)

using rates of $1 and $4 per million input and output tokens, respectively. Requests without matched usage records are counted toward API requests but not token usage or cost. The estimates cover teacher inference, excluding executor, student-serving, and training costs. Student routing also removes unused scalar-head and outer relation-refinement calls.

Savings. We measure reductions in teacher API requests, tokens, and estimated cost relative to the matched teacher:

Reduction(%)\displaystyle\mathrm{Reduction}(\%) =100​(1−x¯studentx¯teacher),\displaystyle=100\left(1-\frac{\overline{x}_{\mathrm{student}}}{\overline{x}_{\mathrm{teacher}}}\right), (9)

where both means are computed over the same set of tasks.

C.3 Statistical Uncertainty

We compute 95% confidence intervals from 200,000 task-level bootstrap samples (seed 0). Performance metrics are resampled within TB2, TB3, and LHTB using fixed weights of 65/11365/113, 23/11323/113, and 25/11325/113. For paired comparisons, both methods use the same resampled tasks from their shared set. Resource metrics use equal task weights. We report θ^±h\hat{\theta}\pm h, where hh is the 95th percentile of |θ^∗−θ^||\hat{\theta}^{*}-\hat{\theta}| across bootstrap samples.

Appendix D Prompts and Structured Interfaces

We present the key prompts for hypothesis generation, evidence-based control, and prospective reasoning. Each role receives relevant task clauses, source code, hypotheses, observations, and attempt history. The excerpts follow the implementation; JSON examples illustrate tool arguments rather than actual traces.

Our running example uses count(n), which should return len(range(n)) but instead returns n + 1. The hypothesis count_inclusive identifies the extra increment, while test_count is the failing test.

D.1 Hypothesis Generation

Input. Numbered task clauses and source lines, current diagnostics, existing candidates, and attempt history.

Key instructions.

Each mechanism must state the concrete behavior that is wrong now, the relevant symbol/data flow, and why it causes observed failure. After a failure, add a materially different mechanism or a narrower child. Do not prescribe old/new code, a patch, or claim a repair is correct.

Structured output. submit_frontiers returns a frontiers array. Each entry specifies the defect, predicted outcome, evidence to collect, source and task references, and target check. Source anchors cover at most 20 lines in one file, and each task reference selects one atomic clause. An optional parent_id links a refinement to an earlier hypothesis.

⬇
{"frontiers": [{
"frontier_id": "count_inclusive",
"mechanism": "count(n) adds one, so counts are too large.",
"predicted_outcome": "test_count passes.",
"evidence_to_collect": "Print count(2).",
"source_evidence_path": "count.py",
"source_evidence_line_ids": ["L1", "L2"],
"claimed_actual_behavior": "Returns n + 1.",
"claimed_required_behavior": "Returns len(range(n)).",
"task_evidence_line_ids": ["T1"],
"claimed_discrepancy": "One extra integer is counted.",
"target_check": "test_count",
"related_paths": ["count.py"],
"parent_id": null
}]}

D.2 Evidence Judgment

Input. The hypothesis, claimed behavior, diagnostic command, output, and return code.

Key instructions.

Judge the hypothesis using only the diagnostic output:

  • •

    contradicted: the output disproves the claimed behavior;

  • •

    consistent: the output confirms the claimed behavior;

  • •

    insufficient: the output is inconclusive (e.g., failed command, timeout, or irrelevant output).

Do not rely on plausibility; if the probe contradicts the claim, label it contradicted.

Structured output. submit_verdicts returns a verdicts array with a frontier ID, verdict, and supporting reason. For a probe returning 3 from count(2):

⬇
{"verdicts": [{
"frontier_id": "count_inclusive",
"verdict": "consistent",
"reason": "count(2) printed 3, matching the claimed extra increment."
}]}

D.3 Prospective Evaluation and Frontier Relations

Input. Prospective evaluation uses candidate packets, current source, relevant task clauses, and portfolio context. Relation inference also considers verifier observations and attempt history.

Local-code instructions.

Use only the candidate packet and relevant source code. Trace local control and data flow; a cited source line does not by itself establish a defect. Predict the outcome of one bounded repair attempt.

Structured output. For each candidate, submit_consequence_factors predicts mechanism validity and four conditional probabilities: progress under a valid or invalid mechanism, large progress given nonfull progress, and full resolution given progress. A separate contract judge predicts violates_contract, satisfies_contract, or insufficient, along with p_mechanism_valid, supporting references, and a causal trace.

Mechanism-probability selection. Let mLm_{L} be the local-code estimate of mechanism validity and mJm_{J} the contract-judge estimate after the consistency checks below. We use

m={mJ,if the judge is valid and decisive,mL,otherwise.m=\begin{cases}m_{J},&\text{if the judge is valid and decisive},\\ m_{L},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (10)

A judgment is decisive when it is violates_contract or satisfies_contract; insufficient, abstention, or schema failure leaves mLm_{L} unchanged. The judge affects only mechanism validity, while the remaining conditional probabilities come from local code.

Outcome composition. Let α\alpha and β\beta denote the probabilities of strict progress under a valid and invalid mechanism, respectively; ff the probability of full resolution given progress; and ℓ\ell the probability of large progress given nonfull progress. All inputs lie in [0,1][0,1]. For one bounded repair attempt,

pprog\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{prog}} =m​α+(1−m)​β,\displaystyle=m\alpha+(1-m)\beta, (11)
pno​change\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{no\ change}} =1−pprog,\displaystyle=1-p_{\mathrm{prog}}, (12)
ppartial\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{partial}} =pprog​(1−f)​(1−ℓ),\displaystyle=p_{\mathrm{prog}}(1-f)(1-\ell), (13)
plarge\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{large}} =pprog​(1−f)​ℓ,\displaystyle=p_{\mathrm{prog}}(1-f)\ell, (14)
pfull\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{full}} =pprog​f.\displaystyle=p_{\mathrm{prog}}f. (15)

Strict progress is any verifier improvement; large progress additionally requires at least 20% of currently failing tests to newly pass without full resolution, and full resolution reaches reward 11. The runtime field expected_progress is pprogp_{\mathrm{prog}}. We set pharm=0p_{\mathrm{harm}}=0 here and handle observed regressions separately through rollback. The mechanism probability mm is distinct from the exploration belief btib_{t}^{i} in Appendix A.2.

Consistency checks and fallback. Before selecting mm, we reconcile the judge’s category, probability, and causal trace using fixed lexical rules. Explicit statements about current-code behavior take precedence. A trace supporting satisfaction sets satisfies_contract and caps mJm_{J} at 0.20.2; a trace supporting violation sets violates_contract and floors mJm_{J} at 0.80.8.

Otherwise, we retain satisfaction only when mJ≤0.35m_{J}\leq 0.35 and violation only when mJ≥0.5m_{J}\geq 0.5. Inconsistent judgments become insufficient with mJ=0.5m_{J}=0.5 and fall back to the local-code estimate. If that estimate is unavailable, we use

(mL,α,β,ℓ,f)=(0.5,0.5,0.1,0.5,0.5).(m_{L},\alpha,\beta,\ell,f)=(0.5,0.5,0.1,0.5,0.5).

A valid decisive judge may replace the default mLm_{L}.

Relation instructions.

Do not infer relations from shared files alone; prefer call/data-flow dependencies over lexical similarity. Use supports when evidence for one candidate strengthens another, requires when acting on one depends on another, conflicts for mutually exclusive claims, and same_mechanism only for shared causes.

Structured output. submit_relations returns directed candidate pairs, relation types, strengths in [0,1][0,1], and rationales. In our example, a second candidate empty_count attributes the failure at n=0n=0 to the same extra increment:

⬇
{"relations": [{
"source_id": "count_inclusive",
"target_id": "empty_count",
"relation": "same_mechanism",
"strength": 0.95,
"rationale": "Both failures arise from the same extra increment."
}]}

Appendix E Qualitative Case Studies

We examine two archived teacher traces to show how BeliefWeaver uses evidence to update candidate beliefs and select executor continuations. The cases include one score-improving repair and one trajectory with no score gain.

Reading the traces.

Figures 3 and 3 follow four stages: failure state, candidate evidence, belief and choice, and execution result. Log excerpts and extracted fields are shown separately from condensed descriptions. The displayed qq values are controller beliefs, and scores are retained-checkpoint test-pass fractions.

Evidence, decisions, and outcomes.

In Figure 3, code evidence contradicts a missing-check hypothesis, shifting selection toward a fuel-propagation candidate. The resulting continuation raises the score while leaving several failures unresolved. In Figure 3, belief updates redirect exploration toward the server-start hypothesis, but the retained score does not improve. Local startup succeeds, while the subsequent controller probe again fails to connect.

Failure analysis.

The failed case highlights a gap between local execution success and retained-checkpoint performance. Later candidates point to session-lifetime or filesystem-persistence issues, but neither is confirmed by the trace.
